--- title: "Historic Footpath: The Nakasendo Way" date: "2026-08-23" categories: [footpath, historic walks, pre-industrial, Japan] --- Kiso Valley, Gifu and Nagano Prefectures, Japan ![](assets/road-to-nagiso.jpeg) Sections of the Nakasendo Way, November 2023. The tiny postal towns of Magome (馬籠宿) and Tsumago (妻籠宿) are the best-known stops along the Nakasendo Way (中山道), a historic route stretching over 500 kilometers from Tokyo to Kyoto.[^1 Kiso Tourism] In 1600s Tokugawa-era Japan, feudal lords were required by the Shogunate to make periodic journeys between their domains and Edo, now modern-day Tokyo. This practice fueled Edo's urban expansion and spurred the development of pre-industrial transportation, communication, and credit networks. In addition to Magome and Tsumago, other Kiso Valley spots like Narai (奈良井宿) and the city of Ena (恵那市) also maintain historic buildings from this era. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Magome, Tsumago, and around: south to Nagoya, north to Matsumoto. ::: ::: ## Tokugawa-era Nakasendo ### The Five Highways The Nakasendo (中山道, literally "central mountain route"), also called the Kisokaido (木曾街道), ran from the Shogunate's military-political capital of Edo to the imperial capital of Kyoto. It was one of the Gokaido (五街道)，five centrally-administered routes fanning out from Edo. ![The Gokaido, or Edo Five Routes. Map by Artanisen, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.](assets/gokaido-edo-five-routes-map.png){width=500 fig-alt="Map of the five Edo-period routes across Japan"} | Route | Final Point | Rough Distance | Postal Stations | Terrain | | ------- | ----------------- | ------------ | ---------------- | --------------- | | Nakasendo (Kisokaido) | Kyoto | ~534 km / 332 mi | 69 stations | Mountainous inland path through central Honshu | | Tokaido | Kyoto | ~514 km / 319 mi | 53 stations | Southern coastal lowland path | | Koshu Kaido | Shimosuwa-shuku, linking to Nakasendo via Kai Province | ~210 km / 130 mi | 44 stations | Hilly route through Kanto plain into the Kai Basin | | Oshu Kaido | Shirakawa, Mutsu Province | ~185 km / 115 mi | 27 stations (first 17 shared with Nikko Kaido) | Northbound plain and low hills | | Nikko Kaido | Nikko Tosho-gu, Shimotsuke Province | ~146 km / 91 mi | 21 stations (first 17 shared with Oshu Kaido) | Flat northbound plain route | These highways are depicted in some of the most iconic artwork of the time. The 53 postal stations of the Tokaido were memorialized in a series by famed woodblock artist, Utagawa Hiroshige, seen in an exhibition at the [Shizuoka City Tokaido Hiroshige Museum of Art](https://tokaido-hiroshige.jp/en/exhibition/2024/fifty-three_stations.html) showing horses, soldiers, porters, servants, and nobles. Hiroshige also partnered with Keisai Eisen and other artists for a woodblock series depicting the Nakasendo's 69 postal stations: first Eisen drew 24 prints, after which Hiroshige took over. The [Nakasendo Hiroshige Museum of Art](https://hiroshige-ena.jp/english/) in Ena City has posted [a helpful guide](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LrUvYMylVl4) to their collection of these prints (turn on English subtitles for translation). ### Alternate Attendance as Political Control The year is 1600. Tokugawa Ieyasu achieves a decisive victory at the Battle of Sekigahara, establishing himself as the supreme military commander, or Shogun, after decades of civil war between feudal clans.[^2 Francks] He forms his government in a small fishing village, Edo, later renamed Tokyo in 1858.[^3 Ito Hoshi] His family will govern Japan without major political crises for more than 250 years,[^4 Ito Hoshi] and Japan's population will more than double, from 12 to 33 million.[^x Francks 29] Now, though, he must consolidate his authority over a fractured country. Introduced in 1635 to prevent rebellion, alternate attendance, or sankin-kotai (参勤交代), helped cement the Tokugawa Shogunate's territorial control.^[x Vaporis 12] The Tokugawa Shogunate was concurrently pushing through other dramatic changes, including sakoku ("locked country," a near-ban on foreign entry and trade that stemmed the outflow of silver to China) and the required construction and refurbishment of domain castle-towns.[^x Francks 22-24] Under alternate attendance, every two years, the Shogunate expected feudal lords, or daimyo, to journey from their domains to spend a year in residence in Edo, where their wives and children lived as effective hostages to guarantee their loyalty.^[5] Owing to alternate attendance and the construction of domainal residences in Edo, the city grew to one of the world's largest urban areas of its time, boasting a population of a million or more by the early 1700s.^[6] Its size led to its moniker of Toto, eastern capital, in contrast with Japan's western capital of Kyoto.^[x Vaporis 128] On a political level, sustaining this practice was a heavy tax on feudal daimyo, who might otherwise amass resources in their domains. The practice occupied much of their time, as daimyo might spend much of their adult lives either in residence at or traveling to and from Edo. The journey could also be lengthy for daimyo of far-flung domains. If setting out from the distant domain of Tosa on the island of Shikoku, it took 3-4 weeks of travel to arrive in Edo.^[7 Vaporis] Moreover, daimyo were expected to travel in a style befitting their status. Historian Constantine Vaporis explains that depending on a domain's distance from Edo, travel costs could equal 5 to 20 percent of its budget.^[8] Adding the hefty expense of supporting a domain's Edo residence and staff, total outlays might consume between half and three-quarters of a domain's disposable income.^[9] From an economic perspective, alternate attendance necessitated the development of the Gokaido, the five long-distance highways, with nearby inns, tea houses, and postal stations to serve as way-stations. As a practical matter, increased official travel also required longer-ranging logistics and communications networks, even forms of payment on credit. Over time, these increased expenses and Japan's economic isolation prompted import substitution and domain-assisted specialization in regional markets. While the domains' fiscal base was officially founded on taxes paid in rice, not all domains were suited to rice cultivation. The more successful domains invested resources to encourage the production and regional trade in high-quality local specialities, including subsidies, technique development, and quality control. Economic historian Penolope Francks details the cultivation of indigo in Tokushima and paper in Tosa, which those daimyo carried with them as promotional advertisements to gift along their travels.[^x Francks 35-39] ::: {.callout-note title="Breaking the Monopoly of the Osaka Wholesalers"} Osaka wholesalers' growing power is a theme that carries through Francks' description of this period. The Tokugawa era's economic insulation and rapid urbanization elevated Osaka's role as a merchant base and supplier to Edo. Osaka served as a trading hub for tax rice (based on land surveys and typically paid in kind), processed goods like soy sauce and sake, and manufactures of products like clothing and ceramics. Consequently, its merchant houses developed commercial and financial expertise in managing regional trade in these goods. Though they received authorization from the Shogun, their monopoly arose in large part because they could offer producers and merchants credit against future purchases.^[Francks 36] One positive result of expanding regional commerce: the declining severity of food shortages and famines that had characterized medieval Japan. However, the wholesalers' market monopoly and price-setting powers were not necessarily welcomed by the regional daimyo, who sought to bypass Osaka and carve out profits for themselves. In her study, Francks identifies daimyo tactics including: * a Tokushima domain-run agency that reserved for itself the middleman power of selling indigo to the wholesalers (a short-lived move protested by local merchants); * the Tokushima establishment of free but centralized trade in indigo within the domain, with local taxes on sales (taken to court by the wholesalers); * a Tosa domain-set licensed monopoly on paper sales above the domain's allotted quota (another short-lived experiment that met local resistance); * Tosa's ultimate abandonment of its quota system, replaced by a more profitable sales and "export" tax on paper. ::: ### Recommended reading Summary narrative above based on the excellent work of: | Author | Title | Year | Description | | ------ | ----- | ---- | ----------- | | Penelope Francks | [_Japanese Economic Development: Theory and Practice, 3rd Edition_](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/26121343-japanese-economic-development) | 2015 | Fascinating history of Japan's economic development from the Tokugawa era until World War II. | | Takatoshi Ito and Takeo Hoshi | [_The Japanese Economy, 2nd Edition_](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262357180/the-japanese-economy/) | 2020 | Seminal text on Japan's economy, with a focus on postwar development. | | Constantine Vaporis | [_Tour of Duty: Samurai, Military Service in Edo, and the Culture of Early Modern Japan_](https://uhpress.hawaii.edu/title/tour-of-duty-samurai-military-service-in-edo-and-the-culture-of-early-modern-japan/) | 2009 | The textbook history on the practice of alternate attendance. | ![](assets/nakasendo-banner-iii.jpeg) ## Trip planning! The tiny Kiso Valley towns of Magome, Tsumago, and Narai are the best-known postal towns along the Nakasedo Way. They see a variety of visitors, from international tourists to local class field trips. The towns have restored the wooden buildings General travel notes: - Reserve any lodging **well in advance,** as much as six months or more. Local inns book out quickly, especially in small towns like Magome and Tsumago. - If you're not comfortable with Japanese, download the Google Translate Japanese language pack (or similar) for offline translation. - Bring cash for your travel and stay, including small bills for food and transportation. As of writing, Japan is still highly cash-dominant, especially outside major cities. - Review local bus and train schedules to plan your time. Transportation can be quite sparse. - If you don't have a local mobile/data plan, purchase an e-sim or local simcard for communications. You may find simcard kiosks in larger train stations like Nagoya. Magome and Tsumago travel notes: Dubbed the "Japanese Alps" by a 19th century British tourist, the Kiso Valley area is quite beautiful, particularly as leaves change color in the fall. The route between Magome and Tsumago follows the [x] river Ena travel notes: Regrettably, I didn't know to include the [city of Ena](https://www.japan-guide.com/ad/ena/) in my trip, but it seems lovely and is home to the Hiroshige Museum of Art, which houses a collection of some 1500 of his woodblock prints. The nearby historic castle town of Iwamura is also accessible by a 30-minute train trip from Ena and boasts art galleries, a sake brewery, and traditional confectionary shops as well as the Iwamura castle ruins. Matsumoto travel notes: Time remaining, Matsumoto to the north is a charming smaller city with number of remarkable historic sites. If traveling on to Matsumoto: - Visit [Matsumoto Castle](https://www.matsumoto-castle.jp/eng/about)! - The castle [was preserved by local residents](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n464VoX1zeE) despite being slated for demolition during the Meiji Restoration. - Contact the wonderful and wonderfully-informative ["Alps Language Service Association"](https://www.npo-alsa.com/home-en) to request an English-language tour of the castle. Their dedicated, knowledgeable volunteers give an in-depth introduction to the castle and city overall. - Magome and Tsumago are accessible by train from Nagoya to the south and from Nagano or Matsumoto to the north. - From Nagoya to the south: take a train to Nakatsugawa and then take a [local bus](https://www.japan-guide.com/bus/kiso.html) to Magome. - From Nagano or Matsumoto to the north: take a train to Nagiso, then either wait for a bus or walk to Tsumago. If time allows, I recommend walking. ### Planning inspiration | Blog or Site | Written/Updated | Post or Article | | ------------ | --------------- | --------------- | | Maris Around the World |
